Bhaiya's Teachings — Knowledge Base (Session 81, English)
The Launch of the Chandravanshi Series: Manu's Two Sons, Janmejaya's Snake Sacrifice, and the Birth of Budh and Ila

Sour ce: a live Ashaeiynn session in which Bhaiya formally launches the "Chandravanshi" teaching series (r eferenced thr oughout the later Chandravanshi installments alr eady pr ocessed in this collection). This session covers why the series begins with Chandravanshi rather than Suryavanshi, King Janmejaya's snake sacrifice and Astika's intervention, the devas-vs-asuras power dynamic (yagna shakti vs. amrit), and the origin stories of Budh (Mer cury) and Ila — explaining the Chandravanshi name itself. This session contains substantial genuine live back-and-forth (r egistration r oll call, audience questions, personal anecdotes, and an extended closing teaching on understanding the guru's gaze), so it is pr ocessed as a full 3-part document.
1. Session Opening and Logistics

Per this teaching's live texture, the session opens with the sangat gathering, brief audio-check banter , and logistics: aura-checking is nearly complete (one more day planned), a registration form is being opened for anyone not yet checked, and the upcoming Purnima and Mahavan (great havan) are announced.
2. Opening Prayer and Sankalp

Per this teaching's live practice, a formal prayer is of fered inviting Hanuman ji Maharaj's grace over the sankalp (resolve) of all registered practitioners, followed by a roll call of registered names for whom collective jaap and prayer are being dedicated that day .
3. A Teaching on Divya Drishti (Divine Sight)

Per this teaching, divya drishti is described as a distinct power that, once attained, opens access to a fuller reality encompassing both the physical world and the astral world — allowing a practitioner to perceive what already exists but is normally invisible to ordinary sight.
4. Launching the Chandravanshi Series
Per this teaching, Bhaiya formally announces the start of a new teaching series, "Chandravanshi," to be followed later by a "Suryavanshi" series.
5. Why Chandravanshi Befor e Suryavanshi

Per this teaching, even though the Ramayana (associated with the Suryavansh) predates the Mahabharata (associated with the Chandravansh) chronologically , understanding the Mahabharata first is presented as a prerequisite for properly understanding the Ramayana — per this teaching, those who claim to understand the Ramayana easily but struggle with the Mahabharata will, in fact, never fully understand the Ramayana either .
6. The Series' Purpose: Recognizing Sants in the Subtle World

Per this teaching, the deeper purpose of learning these stories is that once a practitioner's divya drishti opens, they will begin encountering sants in the subtle world — and without knowing their names, qualities, and stories (drawn from the Vedas and Puranas), a practitioner cannot meaningfully recognize, address, or learn from them; an unrecognized "crowd of sants" is spiritually useless without this foundation.
7. Recap: King Parikshit's Death

Per this teaching, recapping a story told the previous day , King Parikshit, despite hiding out of fear after being cursed to die from snakebite, was killed on the seventh day by a worm hidden inside an apple — the worm was actually Takshak Naga in disguise.
8. Janmejaya's Vow and the Sarpa Satra

Per this teaching, Parikshit's son Janmejaya, enraged, vowed to destroy all nagas and began a "satra" — a mass yagna in which roughly a hundred pandits chant mantras and of fer ahutis (oblations) together — specifically a sarpa satra (snake sacrifice) aimed at exterminating snakes.
9. Rishi Uttanka's Role

Per this teaching, the presiding rishi, Uttanka, was himself an enemy of the nagas (a snake had once stolen a valuable gem belonging to his wife, and he bore the resulting blame) — making him and Janmejaya allies in this cause.
10. The Sacrifice's Terrifying Effect

Per this teaching, as the sarpa satra proceeded, snakes were drawn from all directions into the sacrificial fire and burned in massive numbers, causing widespread panic — though no one dared openly oppose the king.
1 1. Astika's Intervention

Per this teaching, one person did speak up: Astika, introduced as the nephew of Vasuki (king of the nagas, on his mother's side) and son of a human father , Jaratkaru — giving him standing to speak for both nagas and humans.
12. Astika's Argument: The Origin of Vasuki's Grievance

Per this teaching, Astika explains that Vasuki's enmity traces back to Arjuna's destruction of the Khandava forest (to build Indraprastha), which killed and displaced many nagas; Vasuki vowed revenge, which was eventually carried out through Karna's Nagastra (serpent weapon, empowered with Takshak's own naga shakti) aimed at Arjuna during the Mahabharata war .
13. How Krishna and Hanuman Saved Arjuna fr om the Nagastra

Per this teaching, when the devas alerted Krishna to the danger , Krishna signaled Hanuman ji Maharaj (present as the flag-bearer on Arjuna's chariot); Hanuman, without any dramatic action, simply increased his own weight, causing the chariot to sink into the ground just enough that the Nagastra missed its true tar get — Krishna then remarks that just as Hanuman once went to Patal Lok to save Ram and Lakshman, he had now done the same for Krishna himself.
14. Astika's Challenging Question to Janmejaya

Per this teaching, Astika then asks Janmejaya whether he believes the Mahabharata war his ancestors fought was truly just — and when Janmejaya af firms it was, Astika presses further: if so, why do the Kauravas rest in heaven while the Pandavas are said to be in hell? Per this teaching, this question leaves Janmejaya stunned.
15. The Sour ce of This Story: Krishna, Vyasa, Ganesh, and Vaishampayan

Per this teaching, this account originates from Krishna's own words, was composed into the Mahabharata by Ved Vyas (dictated to Ganesh ji, who wrote as Vyas spoke), and was transmitted onward through Vyasa's chief disciple, Rishi Vaishampayan — described as the recurring narrator figure who appears whenever the Mahabharata's telling is depicted, distinct from Vyasa himself.
16. Devas vs. Asuras: The Sour ces of Their Respective Power

Per this teaching, an enduring conflict exists between devas (dwelling above) and asuras (dwelling below); devas maintain their divinity chiefly through yagna shakti (a power granted by Brahma and sustained through ongoing of ferings), while asuras draw power from amrit, said to be found in Patal Lok.
17. Why Asuras Remain Powerful Despite Devas Receiving All Havan Offerings

Per this teaching, although havan ahutis are directed to devatas and never to asuras, asuras nonetheless retain significant power because of their independent access to amrit in Patal Lok — meaning devas' strength is not automatically greater in every respect.
18. Brihaspati's Yagna and the History of Yagna's Decline

Per this teaching, Brihaspati (guru of the gurus, associated with Jupiter/Guru graha) performs the yagna whose ener gy sustains all devas; per this teaching's broader historical aside, yagna was central to ancient practice, with musical/entertainment traditions growing up around long yagna ceremonies to sustain participants' engagement — but by roughly 500 BCE, the yagna practice itself had substantially declined while the storytelling and performance traditions built around it persisted, becoming what we now call "katha" (narrated stories).
19. Tara's Departur e from Brihaspati

Per this teaching, Brihaspati's wife, Tara (described as queen of the tara mandal, the realm of stars), grew frustrated with his highly intellectual, unemotional nature and left him for Chandradev (the moon god), described as emotional and charming; her absence caused Brihaspati's yagnas to stop, weakening the devas and allowing asuras' power to grow .
20. Indra's Intervention and Tara's Return
Per this teaching, Indra, as king of the devas, ordered Tara to return to her husband; she did, but returned pregnant.
21. The Unborn Child's Own Testimony

Per this teaching, in a public assembly , when Tara was asked whose child she carried, she gave no answer — until the unborn child itself spoke from the womb, revealing Chandradev as the true father .
22. Brihaspati's Curse and Indra's Corr ection

Per this teaching, enraged, Brihaspati immediately cursed the unborn child to be neither male nor female; Indra intervened, reminding him that "whoever raises a child is the true father" regardless of the biological parent, and persuaded him to reconsider his anger — many devas then blessed the child to be as wise and intelligent as Brihaspati himself.
23. The Birth of Budh (Mer cury)

Per this teaching, the child, born neither fully male nor female because of the curse, was named Budh — combining Chandra's emotional nature with the discipline and wisdom of the household he was raised in; Budh went on to become ruler of his own graha
(planet), his vahana depicted with an elephant's head and a lion's body , symbolizing a bipolar (dual) nature — a concept this teaching treats as the origin point of "polarity" within this tradition.
24. Manu's Two Sons

Per this teaching, returning to the founding lineage, the first human of each yuga is named Manu; Manu had two sons — Ikshvaku (founder of the Suryavansh, the lineage of Bhagwan Ram) and a second son (per this teaching, associated in Greek mythology with the name "Elias") whose actual name was Sudhamya.
25. Sudhamya's Encounter with Shiva and Parvati

Per this teaching, while hunting, Sudhamya stumbled upon Bhagwan Shiva and Mata Parvati in a private, intimate moment; Parvati requested privacy , and Shiva cast a spell transforming every male being in that forest into female form.
26. Sudhamya's Transformation and Manu's Rejection

Per this teaching, Sudhamya's own gender was altered as a result; Parvati, unable to fully reverse her husband's decree, of fered a partial remedy — Sudhamya would take female form whenever the moon was absent and male form whenever the moon was present. When Manu learned of this, he disowned Sudhamya, who was thereafter known as Ila (or Ilya).
27. Ila and Budh: The Founding of the Chandravanshi Lineage

Per this teaching, while in female form as Ila, Sudhamya was noticed and loved by Budh; their union produced the lineage that became known as the Chandravanshi (lunar dynasty) — with Ikshvaku's line correspondingly known as the Suryavanshi (solar dynasty).
28. A Note on Gr eek and Egyptian Parallels

Per this teaching, Ila's descendants are extensively referenced in Greek mythology under the name "Elias," and Bhaiya of fers a personal aside: during a period of intense sadhna, he and a fellow practitioner ("Ankur Bhaiya") reported perceiving what appeared to be a full sequence of Egyptian deities, which they researched and identified afterward — of fered as an example of how these ancient lineages appear to overlap across dif ferent mythological traditions once divya drishti opens.
29. Why Detailed Names and Stories Matter for Practitioners

Per this teaching, Bhaiya explains he is deliberately naming figures precisely and repeatedly so that practitioners gradually memorize them — since every sant carries their own distinct mantra, yantra, and area of mastery , and recognizing exactly which sant one encounters (rather than treating them as an undif ferentiated "crowd") requires this specific, cumulative knowledge.
30. Encouragement Toward Spiritual Experimentation

Per this teaching's live practice, Bhaiya shares an anecdote about a couple who, during a nighttime astral encounter with a sant, lost roughly 50% of their spiritual ener gy — and rather than being scolded, they were praised for having attempted and experienced something real, in contrast to an overly cautious "stay inside, don't risk anything" mentality Bhaiya associates with typical Indian household caution; genuine growth, per this teaching, requires practiced engagement, not avoidance.
31. A Live Corr ection: Who Is "Queen of Patal"?

Per this teaching's live practice, in response to an audience question about the source of asuras' strength, a sangat member incorrectly guesses that the "queen of Patal" is a Patal-dwelling deity distinct from commonly worshipped devis; Bhaiya corrects this live, confirming it is Mahalakshmi herself, described here as "Patal Nivasini."
32. Shukracharya and Sanjivani Vidya

Per this teaching, Shukracharya, guru to the asuras, obtained Sanjivani Vidya (the power to revive the dead) and used it so extensively on the asuras' behalf that Bhagwan Shiva swallowed him to prevent further misuse, keeping him within his own body for roughly a thousand years until releasing him once the asuras had been brought back under control.
33. Closing Teaching: Bhakti Must Change a Life

Per this teaching's closing reflections, devotion (bhakti) that does not visibly transform a practitioner's life and outlook is described as having no real substance — such unchanged devotion, per this teaching, only inflates ego rather than producing genuine growth.
34. Closing Teaching: Understanding the Guru's Drishti (Gaze)

Per this teaching, a disciple's ultimate goal should be to understand the perspective (drishti) from which their guru sees them — since the way a disciple views their guru reflects their own bhaav (disposition), while the way the guru views the disciple reflects the guru's own bhaav; recognizing and internalizing the guru's own perspective is described as the true marker of spiritual maturity .
35. An Illustrative Anecdote on Understanding a Guru's Hints

Per this teaching, Bhaiya shares a personal anecdote: while in meditation, a figure he addresses as "Manu Bhaiya" appeared, and Bhaiya, pressing him for a specific Ram Katha, instead received an unplanned Shani Dev katha — illustrating, per this teaching, that any guru keeps closest those disciples capable of understanding subtle hints and unspoken direction, not just explicit instruction.
QUICK RULES SUMMARY

The Chandravanshi series is deliberately taught before the Suryavanshi series because, per this teaching, understanding the Mahabharata (Chandravansh) is a prerequisite for properly understanding the Ramayana (Suryavansh), despite the Ramayana's earlier chronological setting. Divya drishti opens access to both the physical and astral worlds; learning the specific names, stories, and qualities of sants (from Vedas and Puranas) is what allows a practitioner to meaningfully recognize and engage with the sants they encounter once this sight opens. King Parikshit died from a disguised Takshak Naga despite hiding from a curse; his son Janmejaya's resulting sarpa satra (mass snake-sacrifice yagna) was halted only after Astika — nephew of naga king Vasuki and son of a human father — challenged Janmejaya's assumption that the Mahabharata war (and its ongoing consequences) represented pure justice. Vasuki's grievance traced to Arjuna's destruction of the Khandava forest; his eventual revenge attempt (via Karna's Nagastra against Arjuna) was thwarted when Krishna signaled Hanuman ji Maharaj, who saved Arjuna simply by increasing his own weight. Devas draw their sustaining power from yagna shakti (granted by Brahma), while asuras draw power independently from amrit found in Patal Lok — explaining why asuras remain powerful despite receiving no havan of ferings. Brihaspati's wife Tara left him for the more emotionally warm Chandradev; their resulting son, cursed by Brihaspati to be neither male nor female (after Indra's intervention prevented a worse outcome), became Budh (Mercury) — his elephantheaded, lion-bodied vahana symbolizing the origin of "polarity" in this tradition. Manu's two sons were Ikshvaku (founder of the Suryavansh) and Sudhamya, whose gender was altered after inadvertently witnessing Shiva and Parvati in private union; as Ila, Sudhamya's union with Budh founded the Chandravanshi (lunar) lineage — paralleling the extensive "Elias" references found in Greek mythology . Genuine spiritual growth, per this teaching, requires active engagement and even occasional setbacks (such as temporary ener gy loss from an astral encounter) rather than excessive caution — devotion that does not visibly transform a person's life is described as producing only ego, not real growth.

A disciple's highest goal is described as coming to understand the drishti (perspective) from which their own guru views them, since recognizing a guru's own bhaav (disposition) — including unspoken hints — is what draws a disciple closer . Spelling note: the institute's name is written "Ashaeiynn" — use this spelling consistently .

Present all mythological/narrative material as "per this teaching," not as settled historical or scriptural fact.
